deep.reconstruction:
Context (no. 82 'Consideratio circa quadrata magica', from the previous page). Euler shifts the entries of a magic square so that every row and column sums to 0. For an odd square he uses the entries 0, ±1, ±2, ...; for an even square, ±1, ±3, .... In §II he defines 'quaterna loca connexa', the four corners of a rectangle (1,2 in one row; 3,4 in another row under 1,2). Writing +a, -a, -a, +a in those corners leaves every row and column sum unchanged. In modern terms this is an elementary 'rectangle move' in the space of matrices with zero line sums.

This page.

§II (end). The move preserves row and column sums. At this stage the diagonal condition (diagonal sums = 0) is not yet imposed.

§III. Method: superpose such rectangle moves, so a cell may carry several letters. Use enough letters that (i) all the required numbers can actually occur and (ii) the diagonal conditions can be met.

§IV. 3×3 square, first attempt, superposing three rectangle moves:
- a on cells (1,1),(1,3),(3,1),(3,3);
- b on (1,2),(1,3),(2,2),(2,3);
- c on (2,1),(2,2),(3,1),(3,2).
The resulting matrix is M = [[a, b, -a-b], [c, -b-c, b], [-c-a, c, a]].
All row and column sums vanish identically.
- Main diagonal: a + (-b-c) + a = 2a - b - c = 0.
- Anti-diagonal: (-a-b) + (-b-c) + (-c-a) = -(2a+2b+2c) = 0. Euler writes 2a+2b+2c = 0, which is equivalent.
Hence b+c = 2a and b+c = -a, so a = 0 and c = -b. The square becomes [[0, b, -b], [-b, 0, b], [b, -b, 0]]. Only three distinct values occur, so 0, ±1, ..., ±4 cannot all appear. Euler: 'hinc numeri propositi obtineri nequeunt.'

§V. Second attempt: leave the centre empty (= 0) and use three rectangles that avoid the centre:
- a on (1,1),(1,3),(3,1),(3,3);
- b on (1,1),(1,2),(3,1),(3,2) with signs +,-,-,+;
- c on (2,1),(2,3),(3,1),(3,3).
The resulting matrix is M = [[a+b, -b, -a], [c, 0, -c], [-a-b-c, b, a+c]].
Line sums are identically 0. Both diagonals give the same condition, 2a + b + c = 0, so c = -2a - b. The cells are:
- I = a+b, II = -b, III = -a;
- IV = -2a-b, V = 0, VI = 2a+b;
- VII = a, VIII = b, IX = -a-b.
The magnitudes needed are |a|, |b|, |a+b|, |2a+b|, which must be {1,2,3,4}. Euler chooses a=1, b=2, giving |a+b| = 3 and |2a+b| = 4.

Next page: the square is [[3,-2,-1], [-4,0,4], [1,2,-3]]. Adding 5 to every entry gives the Lo Shu [[8,3,4], [1,5,9], [6,7,2]] with magic sum 15.

[My remark] Zero-line-sum 3×3 matrices form a 4-dimensional space, spanned by (n-1)² = 4 rectangle moves. The two diagonal conditions cut this to the 2-dimensional space of zero-sum magic squares, whose centre is forced to be 0. Euler's §V family (a, b free) is exactly this whole space. The failure in §IV comes from using only 3 of the 4 needed parameters; it is not a flaw of the method itself.
errors: No computational errors. Every row, column and diagonal sum and every substituted entry checks out.
The anti-diagonal sum in §IV is actually -(2a+2b+2c); Euler writes 2a+2b+2c=0, which is equivalent (a sign convention only).

The verdict in §IV ('numeri propositi obtineri nequeunt') holds only for that particular 3-letter scheme. The scheme spans only a 3-dimensional subspace of the 4-dimensional space of zero-line-sum matrices, and is not general enough. Euler implicitly recognises this by switching schemes in §V, but does not explain it.
The choice a=1, b=2 is given without derivation. One must have {|a|,|b|,|a+b|,|2a+b|} = {1,2,3,4}; (a,b) = (1,2) and its sign and symmetry variants work. This is an easily filled gap, not an error.

results.what: Rectangle (four-corner ±a) move preserving row and column sums, used as building blocks for magic squares
results.modern_name: Elementary moves / basis of the space of matrices with zero row and column sums (cf. transportation polytope, Markov-basis moves)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical; in the magic-square setting Euler, E795 'De quadratis magicis' (1776, publ. 1849) uses related letter methods

results.what: Two-parameter general form of the 3×3 magic square with magic sum 0 (centre 0): [[a+b,-b,-a],[-2a-b,0,2a+b],[a,b,-a-b]]
results.modern_name: Parametrization of 3×3 magic squares (equivalent to Lucas's formula c±a, c±b, c±(a+b), c±(a-b))
results.usually_credited_to: Édouard Lucas (1891) for the standard parametrization; implicit in earlier work

results.what: Derivation of the Lo Shu from the parametrization (a=1, b=2, then add 5)

deep.surprise_reason: This is elementary magic-square algebra, published in Euler's Opera postuma (1862) from the Adversaria, and close to his known paper E795 on magic squares. The 3×3 parametrization is equivalent to Lucas's later formula, but it is simple and implicit in earlier treatments, so its presence here is only a minor curiosity.

checkable.sympy: a,b,c=symbols('a b c'); M=Matrix([[a,b,-a-b],[c,-b-c,b],[-c-a,c,a]]); [simplify(sum(M.row(i))) for i in range(3)]+[simplify(sum(M.col(j))) for j in range(3)]
checkable.asserts: §IV scheme has all row and column sums zero (list of zeros)
Diagonal conditions in §IV force a=0, c=-b
§V diagonals give 2a+b+c and -(2a+b+c), i.e. a single condition
Entries I–IX listed by Euler are correct
a=1, b=2 plus shift 5 yields the Lo Shu

checkable.sympy: L=Matrix([[8,3,4],[1,5,9],[6,7,2]]); [sum(L.row(i)) for i in range(3)]+[sum(L.col(j)) for j in range(3)]+[L.trace(), L[0,2]+L[1,1]+L[2,0]]
checkable.asserts: All eight line sums of the resulting square equal 15

transcription_corrections: Transcription agrees with the image. The second diagonal condition in §IV is indeed printed as 2a+2b+2c=0, and the stacked letters in the cells ('-a -b', '-b -c', '-c -a', '+a +b', '-c -b -a', '+c +a') are rendered correctly.
